title: AI in Excel 3: Claude in Excel

lessons.title: Install and sign in on Mac
learn: Control + Option + C, what Claude can see
lessons.mac:
Open or close Claude: Control + Option + C
Excel for Mac: Insert > Get Add-ins, or Home > Add-ins
Shortcut clash? Check other apps that use Control + Option + C

steps.say: Here's where we'll end up: Claude in Excel open beside a monthly profit sheet, answering questions and pointing to the exact cells it used. Setting it up takes about five minutes.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-02 Done

steps.say: You'll learn where to get the add-in, what plan you need, how to open it with Control Option C, and what Claude can see in your workbook. Practice sheet: S20-02.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Install Claude from Microsoft Marketplace
• Sign in with a paid Claude plan
• Open the pane: Control + Option + C
• What Claude can see and change
Practice sheet: S20-02

steps.say: Claude in Excel is an add-in made by Anthropic. You install it from Microsoft Marketplace, the same store as other Office add-ins. It needs a paid Claude plan: Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise. The free plan won't sign in.

acts.t:
Before you start
• Add-in: Claude by Anthropic, from Microsoft Marketplace
• Plan: Claude Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise (paid)
• Work laptop: IT may need to allow or deploy the add-in
• Works in Excel for Mac, Windows and the web

steps.say: Open sheet S20-02. It's a simple monthly profit sheet: revenue, expenses, profit and margin for April 2025 to March 2026, with totals in row 14.
To install, go to the Home tab and click Add-ins. On Excel for Mac you can also use Insert, Get Add-ins.
Click More Add-ins to open the store. In the search box, type Claude and press Return.

Look for Claude by Anthropic. Check the publisher name before you click Add. Copycat add-ins exist, and you're giving this one access to your data. We already have it installed, so I'll close the store.
The first time you open it, Claude asks you to sign in with your Claude account in a small window. After that, it remembers you on this Mac.

acts.t:
First launch
1. Click Add, accept the permissions
2. Open Claude from the Home tab (or Control + Option + C)
3. Sign in with your Claude account (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise)
4. The pane opens on the right

steps.say: Now open it. On a Mac, press Control Option C. In Excel for the web you can also click the Claude button on the Home tab. Let's ask what it can see.

acts.t: What can you see in this workbook? List the sheets briefly, then for sheet S20-02 tell me what each column holds and what the FY total profit is.

steps.say: Claude reads the whole workbook, not only the selected cells. Its answer lists the sheets and describes S20-02, and it mentions cell addresses like D14. Those addresses are citations. You can click them to jump to the cell.
Let's verify the citation. Click D14, the FY total profit. It shows ₹51,47,000. Read the formula bar: it's a SUM of D2 to D13. Claude's figure should match.
One more check. Ask Claude how it calculated the April profit. It should point you to D2 and say revenue minus expenses.

acts.t: How is the April profit in D2 calculated? Don't change anything.

steps.say: Click D2. It shows ₹3,78,000, and the formula is B2 minus C2. Claude's explanation and the sheet agree.
What can Claude change? It can write formulas, add sheets, charts and PivotTables. For anything larger than a small edit, it asks first and tells you what it will change. You stay in control.

acts.t:
What Claude can do
• Read every sheet, formula and value
• Explain with cell citations
• Edit cells, add sheets, charts, PivotTables
• Asks before larger edits; you approve
• Command Z undoes its edits

steps.say: A common mistake is installing it while signed in to Excel with a personal account, then wondering why the work file doesn't show it. Add-ins follow the Microsoft account you're signed in with.

acts.t:
Common mistake
Add-in missing in a work file?
• Check File > Account: are you in your work account?
• Ask IT if add-ins from Marketplace are blocked
• Restart Excel after installing

steps.say: On Excel for Mac, Control Option C opens and closes the pane. If the shortcut does nothing, open it once from the ribbon. Some Mac keyboard tools use the same keys.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Open or close Claude: Control + Option + C
Excel for Mac: Insert > Get Add-ins, or Home > Add-ins
Shortcut clash? Check other apps that use Control + Option + C

steps.say: To recap. Install Claude by Anthropic from Microsoft Marketplace and sign in with a paid plan. Open it with Control Option C. And click the cells it cites to check its answers.

acts.t:
Recap
• Marketplace add-in, paid Claude plan
• Control + Option + C opens the pane
• It reads the whole workbook; click its citations to check

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Claude which month had the lowest profit margin, then click the cell it cites and confirm it with MIN on column E. Compare with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Claude: which month had the lowest profit margin?
Click the cell it cites; confirm with =MIN(E2:E13).
Compare with sheet S20-02 Done.

steps.say: This is the result: a one-page map of an inherited workbook, showing which sheet feeds which and where the key numbers live. Plus a list of problems we spotted on the way. Claude drafted it, and we checked each line.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-03 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to get a walk-through of a multi-sheet workbook with cell citations, trace a key number back to its inputs, and write a map of how the sheets connect. Practice sheets: the four sheets that start with S20-03.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Ask for a walk-through with cell citations
• Trace a number back to its inputs
• Build a map of how sheets connect
Practice: S20-03, S20-03 Inputs, S20-03 Sales, S20-03 Costs

steps.say: Picture this. A colleague leaves, and you get their monthly P and L file for Shree Ganesh Traders, a rice, oil and dal wholesaler in Nagpur. Four sheets, hundreds of formulas, no notes.
Here's how it looks: inputs, a sales sheet, a costs sheet and this summary. Instead of clicking through every formula, ask Claude for a guided tour.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-03 Inputs
Go to the sheet S20-03 Sales
Go to the sheet S20-03 Costs

steps.say: Open Claude with Control Option C. Ask: walk me through the sheets whose names start with S20-03. Explain what each one does and how they connect, citing cells. Don't change anything.

acts.t: Walk me through the sheets whose names start with S20-03. Explain what each sheet does and how they connect, citing the key cells. Do not change anything.

steps.say: Claude describes each sheet and the flow: inputs feed the costs, sales feed costs and the summary, and the summary adds it all up. Notice the cell references in its answer. Each one is a link.
Now trace one number. Ask: how is FY EBITDA in cell N11 of sheet S20-03 calculated? Trace it back to the inputs, step by step.

acts.t: How is FY EBITDA in cell N11 of sheet S20-03 calculated? Trace it back to the input cells step by step, citing each cell.

steps.say: Follow the trail yourself. Click N11 on the summary sheet and read the formula bar. It adds row 11 across the months.
Look closely at the range. It says B11 to L11. The months run from B to M. March is missing. Claude may have flagged this already. If not, you just found it yourself.
Keep tracing. EBITDA in each month depends on the costs sheet. Go to S20-03 Costs and click E3, the May commission. It shows zero, because the formula points to an empty input cell.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-03 Costs

steps.say: Ask Claude to note problems without fixing them: list anything in these S20-03 sheets that looks wrong, with the cell, but don't fix it. We'll fix them in the next lesson.

acts.t: List anything in the S20-03 sheets that looks wrong or risky, such as error values, ranges that miss months, inconsistent formulas or typed numbers. Give the cell for each. Do not fix anything.

steps.say: Read the list against the sheet. A good answer mentions the October revenue in the Sales sheet, the commission formulas, an error in July and the March gap. Claude may phrase them differently.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-03 Sales

steps.say: Now check one number the old-fashioned way. On the summary sheet, in B15, type equals SUM, open bracket, then the S20-03 Sales sheet, H2 colon H13, close bracket.

acts.h: Type =SUM('S20-03 Sales'!H2:H13) and press Return

steps.say: B15 shows ₹10,15,68,825, the same as N2. So the summary agrees with the Sales sheet. That doesn't prove Sales is right, as we saw with October, but the link between the sheets works.
Finally, ask for the map. Ask Claude to write a short map of how the S20-03 sheets connect, as a table you can paste into a documentation sheet.

acts.t: Write a short map of how the S20-03 sheets connect: one row per sheet with what it holds, what it feeds, and its key cells. Give it as a table I can paste. Do not change the workbook.

steps.say: Compare its table with the Done sheet. The best maps name the key cells, so the next person can check them. Copy the table into a sheet called Notes in your own file.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-03 Done

steps.say: A common mistake is asking Claude about a file that has many unrelated sheets, without saying which ones you mean. It reads everything, so name the sheets in your prompt.

acts.t:
Common mistake
Vague: “Explain this workbook.”
Better: “Walk me through the sheets whose names start with S20-03 …”
Name the sheets, the cell, and say “do not change anything” when you only want to read.

steps.say: To recap. Ask for a walk-through with citations. Trace one key number back to its inputs and click every citation. And save a map of the sheets for the next person.

acts.t:
Recap
• Walk-through: what each sheet does, how they connect
• Trace: follow N11 back to the inputs
• Map: one row per sheet, key cells, saved in the file

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Claude where the salary increase in October comes from, and follow the citations to the input cell. Compare with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Claude: where does the October salary increase come from?
Follow the citations to 'S20-03 Inputs'!B5.
Compare with sheet S20-03 Done.

steps.say: Here's the fix log. Four problems in an inherited P and L: a reference error, a total that misses March, a typed revenue figure and a commission formula that drifts. Claude found each one, and we approved each fix.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-04 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to ask Claude for an error review, approve fixes one at a time, and check each fix yourself. Practice sheets: the four sheets that start with S20-04.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Ask for a review: errors, wrong ranges, typed numbers
• Approve each fix, one at a time
• Check every fix and the final totals
Practice: S20-04, S20-04 Inputs, S20-04 Sales, S20-04 Costs

steps.say: Three kinds of problem cause most spreadsheet mistakes. Error values that everyone can see. Ranges that miss rows or months, which look fine. And typed numbers sitting where a formula should be.

acts.t:
What to look for
1. Error values: #REF!, #DIV/0!, #N/A, #VALUE!
2. Wrong ranges: a SUM that stops a row or a month early
3. Typed numbers: a constant where a formula should be
4. Missing $: a reference that drifts when copied

steps.say: Open sheet S20-04. Notice the hash REF error in July other expenses, E9, and how it spreads into the totals in column N.
Open Claude and ask: check the sheets whose names start with S20-04 for errors, wrong ranges, inconsistent formulas and typed numbers. List each problem with its cell. Don't change anything yet.

acts.t: Check the sheets whose names start with S20-04 for error values, ranges that miss rows or months, formulas that are inconsistent with their neighbours, and typed numbers where a formula should be. Number each problem and give its cell. Do not change anything yet.

steps.say: Claude returns a numbered list. Check it covers the hash REF in July, the FY EBITDA range, the October revenue in the Sales sheet and the commission column in Costs. The order and wording will vary.
Approve one fix at a time. Ask: fix the hash REF error in E9 first. Tell me what you'll change before you do it.

acts.t: Fix the #REF! error in cell E9 of sheet S20-04 first. Tell me what you will change before you change it.

steps.say: Claude explains the change, usually that E9 should point to the July row of the costs sheet, like its neighbours. If that's right, approve it.

acts.t: Yes, go ahead with that fix.

steps.say: Check it. Click E9. The formula should now match D9 and F9, just one month along. The hash REF in the totals is gone.
Next, the March gap. Ask Claude to fix the FY EBITDA total in N11 so it includes all twelve months, then approve.

acts.t: Now fix the FY EBITDA total in N11 of sheet S20-04 so it includes all twelve months. Tell me the change, then go ahead.

steps.say: Click N11. The formula should now run from B11 to M11.
Now the typed number. Ask Claude to replace the typed October revenue in S20-04 Sales, H8, with the same formula as the other months.

acts.t: Replace the typed October revenue in cell H8 of sheet S20-04 Sales with the same formula used in the other rows of column H. Tell me the old and new value, then go ahead.

steps.say: Go to S20-04 Sales and click H8. It's a formula now. The old typed figure was ₹97,86,380, the formula gives ₹98,23,880. Someone forgot to update it after correcting the units.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-04 Sales

steps.say: Last, the commission. Ask Claude to fix the commission formulas in S20-04 Costs so every month uses the commission rate in Inputs B7.

acts.t: Fix the commission formulas in column E of sheet S20-04 Costs so every month uses the commission rate in 'S20-04 Inputs'!B7 with an absolute reference. Tell me the change, then go ahead.

steps.say: Click E3 on the costs sheet. The rate reference now has dollar signs, dollar B dollar 7, and May's commission is no longer zero.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-04 Costs

steps.say: Now the final check. Back on S20-04, in B15 type equals SUM of the Sales sheet H2 to H13, and compare it with N2.

acts.h: Type =SUM('S20-04 Sales'!H2:H13) and press Return

steps.say: Both show ₹10,16,06,325. And FY EBITDA in N11 is now ₹1,05,03,444, matching the Done sheet. Every fix is visible in a formula you can read.

A common mistake is saying: fix everything. Claude may make several changes at once, and it's hard to check what changed. One fix per message keeps the review easy, and Command Z can undo any single step.

acts.t:
Common mistake
“Fix all the errors” in one go.
• Ask for a numbered list first
• Approve one fix per message
• Check each cell before the next fix
• Command Z undoes a change

steps.say: To recap. Ask for a numbered review without changes. Approve fixes one at a time. And finish with a hand total that matches.

acts.t:
Recap
• Review first: errors, ranges, typed numbers, missing $
• One fix per message, approve, then check the cell
• Finish with a hand check of the key totals

steps.say: Your challenge: in the S20-03 sheets, make the same four fixes yourself, without Claude, and compare your FY EBITDA with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
Fix the same four problems in the S20-03 sheets by hand.
Your FY EBITDA should match sheet S20-04 Done, cell B11.

steps.say: Here's the cleaned customer master: proper-case names, ten-digit phone numbers, official state names, real dates and upper-case GSTINs. Column G lists every change, so anyone can audit it.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-05 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to clean names, phones, states and dates with one clear prompt, keep the original untouched, and check the result. Practice sheet: S20-05.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Standardise names, phones, states, dates, GSTINs
• Keep the original; clean into a new sheet
• Add a Changes column as an audit trail
• Check row counts and a few rows by eye
Practice sheet: S20-05

steps.say: The golden rule for cleaning with AI: never overwrite your only copy. Ask for the cleaned data on a new sheet, with a column that says what changed. Then you can compare line by line.

acts.t:
Clean safely
1. Keep the original sheet as it is
2. Cleaned copy on a new sheet
3. A Changes column: what changed in each row
4. Check: same number of rows, spot-check 3 rows

steps.say: Open sheet S20-05. Twenty-two customers. Look at the mess: extra spaces, capital letters, phones with plus nine one and dashes, state codes like MH and U.P., old names like Orissa, and dates in six formats.
Open Claude and give one detailed prompt. Clean the customer list on sheet S20-05 into a new sheet called S20-05 Clean, with the rules for each column, and a Changes column. Don't touch the original.

acts.t: Clean the customer list on sheet S20-05 into a new sheet called S20-05 Clean. Keep the same columns in the same order, header in row 1. Rules: Customer name in proper case with extra spaces removed, keep Pvt. Ltd. as written; Phone as digits only, 10 digits for mobiles, landlines with STD code and no leading +91; State as the full official Indian state or union territory name (Orissa becomes Odisha, Pondicherry becomes Puducherry); Onboarded on as a real date shown DD-MM-YYYY, all dates are day first; GSTIN in upper case. Add a column G called Changes that lists what you changed in each row. Do not change sheet S20-05.

steps.say: Claude describes its plan and asks before making a larger change like a new sheet. Read the plan, then approve.

acts.t: Yes, go ahead.

steps.say: Go to the new S20-05 Clean sheet. Scan each column. The states should all be full names, and the dates should be right-aligned, which means Excel sees them as real dates.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-05 Clean

steps.say: Now spot-check three rows against the original. Row 2 was Sharma Electricals in Pune, state MH, date 03 slash 04 slash 2026. It should now read Maharashtra and third April 2026, not fourth March.
Row 13 was Gurgaon with the code HR. That's Haryana. And row 15, Pondy Textiles, should say Puducherry. Read the Changes column for each.
Now count the rows. Go back to sheet S20-05. In I2 type equals COUNTA, open bracket, A2 colon A23, close bracket.
In I3 type equals COUNTA of the S20-05 Clean sheet, A2 colon A100. Both should say twenty-two. If the clean sheet has fewer, Claude dropped a row, maybe one it thought was a duplicate.

acts.h: Type =COUNTA('S20-05 Clean'!A2:A100) and press Return

steps.say: I2 shows 22. Also check that the original is untouched. Click A2: it still has the extra spaces, exactly as we started.
A common mistake is leaving dates ambiguous. Zero three slash zero four can mean third April or fourth March. Always say day first in the prompt, and check one date where the day is twelve or less.

acts.t:
Common mistake
Ambiguous dates: 03/04/2026
• India: 3 April. US: 4 March
• Say “all dates are day first” in the prompt
• Check a date with day ≤ 12 after cleaning

steps.say: A pro tip: ask Claude to keep a short list of every state code it converted, as a small lookup table. Next month you can reuse that table with XLOOKUP, without any AI.

acts.t:
Pro tip
Ask: “Add a small table of every state code you converted and its full name.”
Reuse it next month with XLOOKUP, no AI needed.

steps.say: To recap. Clean into a new sheet and keep the original. Ask for a Changes column as an audit trail. And check the row count, one tricky date and a few rows by eye.

acts.t:
Recap
• New sheet for clean data; original untouched
• Changes column = audit trail
• Check: row count, day-first dates, 3 rows

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Claude to flag any GSTIN whose first two digits don't match the state code for its State. Check one by hand. In this list they should all match.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Claude: flag GSTINs whose first two digits don't match the State (27 = Maharashtra, 29 = Karnataka …).
Check one by hand. In this list, all should match.

lessons.title: Build a model from a description
learn: Budget and forecast with live formulas

steps.say: This is a full-year budget for a cloud kitchen in Pune: inputs at the top, monthly calculations below, and FY totals on the right. Claude built it from an eleven-line brief, with every number driven by the input cells.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-06 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to turn a written brief into a working model with inputs, calculations and outputs, check that it uses live formulas, and test it. Practice sheet: S20-06.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Describe a model in plain English
• Ask for inputs, calculations, outputs
• Insist on live formulas, no typed numbers
• Test it: change an input, hand-check one month
Practice sheet: S20-06

steps.say: Good models have three zones. Inputs, the numbers you might change. Calculations, which only use inputs and other calculations. And outputs, like EBITDA. Tell Claude where each zone goes.

acts.t:
Model layout
Inputs: A3:B11, one per row, yellow
Calculations: months across from column B, row 13 down
Outputs: EBITDA row and FY total in column N
Rule: every calculation refers to an input cell

steps.say: Open sheet S20-06. The brief is in A1 to A11: orders per day, growth, average order value, days, food cost, platform commission, rent, salaries and marketing.
Open Claude and ask it to build the model. Read the brief in A1 to A11 and build a monthly budget for April 2026 to March 2027 on a new sheet called S20-06 Model, with the layout we just described.

acts.t: Read the brief in A1:A11 of sheet S20-06. Build a monthly budget for April 2026 to March 2027 on a new sheet called S20-06 Model. Put the nine inputs in A3:B11 in the same order as the brief, labels in column A and values in column B. Put month headers in row 13 from column B to M, an FY total in column N, and the calculations below: orders per day, orders in month, revenue, food cost, platform commission, contribution, rent, salaries, marketing, EBITDA and EBITDA margin. Every calculation must use live formulas that refer to the input cells. No typed numbers in the calculations.

steps.say: Claude summarises what it will build and asks before creating the sheet. Read the summary. Does it list all nine inputs? Then approve.

acts.t: Yes, go ahead and build it.

steps.say: Go to the new S20-06 Model sheet. Look at the three zones. The inputs should be in A3 to B11 and the months across row 13.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-06 Model

steps.say: Click a calculation cell, for example April revenue, and read the formula bar. You want references to input cells like B5, not a typed four hundred and twenty.

acts.t: Which cell holds April revenue on sheet S20-06 Model, and what is its formula?

steps.say: Now test it. Click B3, orders per day, and type 200. Press Return. Every month and the FY EBITDA should change. If a cell doesn't move, it has a typed number.
Press Command Z to put it back to 180.
Now hand-check April. Go back to sheet S20-06. In A14 type equals 180 star 30 star 420, and press Return.
A14 shows ₹22,68,000. April revenue on the model should be exactly the same. Then check one cost line the same way, for example food cost at thirty-two percent.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-06 Model

steps.say: For reference, the Done sheet shows FY EBITDA of ₹71,96,884. If your model is far off, ask Claude to compare its rows with the brief one by one.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-06 Done

steps.say: A common mistake is accepting a model with typed numbers inside the calculations. It looks right today, and breaks the day someone changes an input. The input test catches it every time.

acts.t:
Common mistake
Typed numbers inside calculations.
• Test: change one input, every linked cell must move
• Ask: “List any calculation cell that contains a typed number.”

steps.say: To recap. Give Claude a brief and an exact layout. Approve, then read the formulas. And test by changing an input and hand-checking one month.

acts.t:
Recap
• Brief + layout: inputs, calculations, outputs
• Live formulas only; read a few
• Test an input, hand-check April

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Claude to add a cash row showing a one-time kitchen setup cost of eight lakh rupees in April as a new input, and check the cumulative cash in March by hand.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Claude: add an input for a one-time setup cost of ₹8,00,000 in April and a cumulative cash row.
Check March cumulative cash by hand:
FY EBITDA (N23) minus ₹8,00,000.

lessons.title: Scenarios and sensitivity with Claude
learn: Change one assumption, trace the impact

steps.say: Here's the cloud kitchen budget again, now with a scenario switch. Type 1, 2 or 3 in Q2 and the whole model flips between base, best and worst cases. Claude built the switch, and helped us see which input matters most.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-07 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to ask what-if questions, trace the impact of one assumption, and build best and worst cases with a switch cell. Practice sheet: S20-07.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Ask a what-if and trace the impact
• Change an input yourself and undo it
• Build Base / Best / Worst with a switch cell
• Find the input that moves EBITDA most
Practice sheet: S20-07

steps.say: A scenario changes several inputs together, like a bad year. A sensitivity changes one input at a time to see how much it matters. Both need a model where everything flows from the inputs.

acts.t:
Scenario vs sensitivity
Scenario: change several inputs together (Best, Worst)
Sensitivity: change one input, measure the effect
Both rely on: inputs → calculations → EBITDA

steps.say: Open sheet S20-07. Inputs are in A3 to B11. FY EBITDA is in N23, currently ₹71,96,884. Platform commission, twenty-two percent, is in B8.
Ask Claude a what-if: if platform commission in B8 goes from twenty-two to twenty-five percent, what happens to FY EBITDA in N23? Trace which rows change. Don't edit anything.

acts.t: On sheet S20-07, if platform commission in B8 goes from 22% to 25%, what happens to FY EBITDA in N23? Trace which rows change and by how much. Do not edit anything.

steps.say: Claude explains the chain: commission rises, contribution falls, and EBITDA falls by three percent of revenue. Note its EBITDA figure. Now let's test it ourselves.
Click B8, type 25 percent, and press Return.
N23 now shows ₹62,31,259. That's about ₹9,65,626 less. Compare with Claude's answer. Then press Command Z to undo.
Now the scenarios. Ask Claude to add a block in P4 to S8 with Base, Best and Worst values for orders per day, growth, average order value and food cost, and a switch cell in Q2.

acts.t: On sheet S20-07, add a scenario block: a label in P2 and a switch cell in Q2 where I type 1, 2 or 3. In P4:S8 put a table with headers Input, Base, Best, Worst and rows for Orders per day (180, 210, 150), Monthly growth in orders (3%, 4%, 1.5%), Average order value (420, 450, 390) and Food cost % (32%, 30%, 35%). Then make B3, B4, B5 and B7 pick their value from the chosen column using the switch. Ask before you change anything.

steps.say: Claude describes the change: a scenario table and formulas like CHOOSE in the four input cells. Approve it.

acts.t: Yes, go ahead.

steps.say: Click B3 and read the formula. It should refer to Q2 and to the scenario table. The yellow inputs are now driven by the switch.
Try it. Click Q2, type 3 for the worst case, and press Return. Watch revenue and EBITDA fall across all twelve months.
Now type 2 for the best case, then 1 to return to the base case. N23 should go back to exactly where it started.
Last, sensitivity. Ask: which single input moves FY EBITDA the most for a ten percent change? Show the numbers for each input. Don't change the sheet.

acts.t: On sheet S20-07, for each input in B3:B11, what would FY EBITDA in N23 be if that input alone were 10% worse? Rank the inputs by impact. Do not change the sheet.

steps.say: Claude ranks the inputs. Usually orders per day and average order value come first, because they drive revenue. Test the top one yourself, the same way we tested commission, and undo.

A common mistake is leaving the switch on the worst case and sending the file. Your manager sees worst-case numbers as the plan. Always label the switch clearly and set it back to base before sharing.

acts.t:
Common mistake
Sharing the file with the switch on 2 or 3.
• Label Q2: “Scenario (1 Base, 2 Best, 3 Worst)”
• Set it to 1 before sending
• Optional: show the active case name in the title

steps.say: To recap. Ask what-ifs and test them by changing the input yourself. Use a switch cell for best and worst cases. And rank inputs by impact to know where to focus.

acts.t:
Recap
• What-if: ask, then test and undo
• Scenarios: one switch cell drives several inputs
• Sensitivity: rank inputs by their effect on EBITDA

steps.say: Your challenge: add a fourth scenario called Monsoon slump, with orders per day of 140 for the whole year, and check its April revenue by hand.

acts.t:
Challenge
Add a 4th case “Monsoon slump”: orders/day 140.
Check April revenue by hand: 140 × 30 × ₹420 = ₹17,64,000.
The Done sheet shows how the switch is built.

lessons.title: From PDF to Excel, and Excel to PowerPoint
learn: Pull a table from a PDF statement

steps.say: Here's the result: a September bank statement, pulled out of a PDF into a clean table, categorised, totalled and checked against the bank's own summary to the paisa. Plus a spending chart ready for a slide.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-08 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to extract a table from a PDF with Claude, categorise transactions, reconcile against the PDF's totals, and draft slides from the numbers. Practice sheet: S20-08.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Attach a PDF and extract its table
• Categorise transactions
• Reconcile with the PDF totals
• Draft summary slides from your numbers
Practice sheet: S20-08 + data/Sahyadri_Bank_Statement_Sep2026.pdf

steps.say: The statement is a sample from a fictional bank, Sahyadri Bank, for one savings account in September 2026. It has twenty-two transactions and a summary box at the bottom with totals. That box is our answer key.

acts.t:
The PDF
Sahyadri Bank Ltd (fictional), sample statement
Account holder: Meera Patil, Sep 2026
22 transactions + a summary box:
opening, total withdrawals, total deposits, closing balance

steps.say: Open sheet S20-08. Column B has the totals typed from the PDF's summary box. Column C is for our totals from the extracted data, and column D shows the difference.
Open Claude. Click the paperclip in the Claude pane and attach the statement PDF from the course data folder.

acts.t: I am attaching a PDF bank statement next. Please wait for my instructions before doing anything.

steps.say: Now the prompt. Extract every transaction into a new sheet called S20-08 Statement, columns A to F: Date, Description, Reference, Debit, Credit and Balance. Skip the opening balance line.

acts.t: From the attached PDF bank statement, extract every transaction into a new sheet called S20-08 Statement. Columns A to F: Date, Description, Reference, Debit, Credit, Balance. Header in row 1, one row per transaction, starting in row 2. Skip the OPENING BALANCE line. Dates as real Excel dates (they are DD-MM-YYYY), amounts as numbers, Reference as text so long numbers are not rounded.

steps.say: Claude asks before creating the sheet. Approve it.

acts.t: Yes, go ahead.

steps.say: Look at the new sheet. Check three things: the reference numbers didn't turn into scientific notation, the dates are real dates, and the last balance is ninety-one thousand one hundred and forty-one rupees and ten paise.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-08 Statement

steps.say: Now reconcile. Back on sheet S20-08, in C2 type equals SUM of the S20-08 Statement sheet, column D.

acts.h: Type =SUM('S20-08 Statement'!D:D) and press Return

steps.say: In C3, the sum of column E. In C4, the closing balance: B7 minus C2 plus C3. In C5, the count: COUNTA of column A minus one for the header.

acts.h: Type =SUM('S20-08 Statement'!E:E) and press Return
Type =COUNTA('S20-08 Statement'!A:A)-1 and press Return

steps.say: Look at column D. Every difference should be zero. Total withdrawals are ₹1,05,338.15, matching the PDF. If any line isn't zero, a transaction was missed or read twice.
Now categorise. Ask Claude to add a Category column G, using simple groups like Salary, Rent, EMI, Food, Groceries, Utilities, Travel, Investments, Cash and Transfer.

acts.t: On sheet S20-08 Statement, add a column G called Category. Use only these categories: Salary, Other income, Interest, Refund, Rent, EMI, Insurance, Investments, Food, Groceries, Utilities, Travel, Health, Shopping, Cash, Transfer. Base it on the Description.

steps.say: Spot-check. The ATM withdrawal should be Cash, the IMPS to self should be Transfer, not spending, and the Amazon refund should be Refund.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-08 Statement

steps.say: Now Excel to PowerPoint. Ask Claude to summarise spending by category on a new sheet with a bar chart, and draft three slides: a title, key numbers, and top spending categories.

acts.t: Create a sheet called S20-08 Summary with total Debit by Category (exclude Transfer) as a table with SUMIFS formulas, and a bar chart of it. Then draft text for 3 slides: 1) title, 2) key numbers for September (income, spending, closing balance), 3) top 3 spending categories with amounts. Use only numbers from the workbook and cite the cells.

steps.say: Check every number in the slide draft against the sheet. Claude cites cells, so click a few. Then copy the chart and text into PowerPoint. If you also use Claude in PowerPoint, it can build the slides from the same numbers.

acts.t:
Excel to PowerPoint
• Check each number in the draft against its cited cell
• Copy the chart (Command C) and paste into PowerPoint (Command V)
• With Claude in PowerPoint, ask it to build the 3 slides from this workbook
• Keep the reconciliation sheet as backup

steps.say: A common mistake is skipping the reconciliation. PDF extraction can drop a line that breaks across pages, or read a balance as a debit. The summary box in the PDF is free proof. Always use it.

acts.t:
Common mistake
Trusting a PDF extract without totals.
• Compare total Dr, total Cr, closing balance, row count
• A difference = a missing or doubled line
• Long reference numbers: keep as text

steps.say: Never upload statements from a source you don't trust, and remember that a PDF can contain hidden instructions. Claude treats file content as data, but you should still read what it plans to do before approving.

acts.t:
Safety
• Bank statements are personal data: follow your company policy
• Untrusted PDFs can hide instructions in the text
• Read Claude's plan before approving edits

steps.say: To recap. Attach the PDF and ask for exact columns. Reconcile totals and row count against the PDF summary. And check every number before it goes on a slide.

acts.t:
Recap
• Extract with exact columns and rules
• Reconcile: Dr, Cr, closing balance, count all match
• Categorise, chart, draft slides; check the cited cells

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Claude for the share of spending on Food and Groceries combined, and check it with SUMIFS on your Category column. Compare with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Claude: what share of September spending (excluding Transfer) was Food + Groceries?
Check with SUMIFS.
Compare with sheet S20-08 Done.

steps.say: Here's the result. One messy expense list cleaned twice, once by Copilot and once by Claude, and a short comparison of how each one worked and how much checking it needed.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-10 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to give both assistants the same prompt, compare their results, and decide which to use for which job. Practice sheets: S20-10 for Copilot and S20-10 Claude for Claude.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Run the same prompt in Copilot and in Claude
• Compare: what changed, formulas or values
• Compare the checking effort
Practice: S20-10 (Copilot), S20-10 Claude (Claude)

steps.say: Both sheets hold the same eighteen July expenses. Vendor names are inconsistent, dates come in six formats, and half the categories are blank.
First, note the total so we can prove nothing was lost. In K2 type equals SUM, open bracket, D2 colon D19, close bracket.
K2 shows ₹50,951. Cleaning must not change this.
Now Copilot, in Edit mode. The prompt: standardise vendor names, convert dates to DD-MM-YYYY, fill blank categories from the description, and add totals by category in G1 to H8. Don't change Amount.

acts.t: On this sheet: standardise the Vendor names (for example SWIGGY LTD and swiggy become Swiggy), convert Date to real dates shown as DD-MM-YYYY (all dates are day first), fill the blank Category cells using the Description with one of Meals, Travel, Hotel, Office supplies, Phone and internet, and add a table of total Amount by Category in G1:H8. Do not change the Amount column.

steps.say: Look at what Copilot did. Check the vendor column, a date with a day of twelve or less, and the new totals table.
Check the totals. In K3 type equals SUM, open bracket, H2 colon H8, close bracket. It should match K2.
Now the same prompt for Claude, on the S20-10 Claude sheet. Open Claude with Control Option C and paste the same instructions, naming the sheet.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S20-10 Claude

acts.t: On sheet S20-10 Claude: standardise the Vendor names (for example SWIGGY LTD and swiggy become Swiggy), convert Date to real dates shown as DD-MM-YYYY (all dates are day first), fill the blank Category cells using the Description with one of Meals, Travel, Hotel, Office supplies, Phone and internet, and add a table of total Amount by Category in G1:H8. Do not change the Amount column.

steps.say: Claude usually describes the changes first and asks before editing. Approve.

acts.t: Yes, go ahead.

steps.say: Same checks. Total in K2, and the category totals in K3.
Now compare the two sheets on four points. Did it ask before editing? Are the totals formulas or typed values? Did it explain what it changed? And how long did your checks take?

acts.t:
Compare
1. Asked before editing?
2. Category totals: formulas (SUMIFS) or typed values?
3. Explained the changes, with cells?
4. Your checking time
Click a total cell on each sheet to answer 2.

steps.say: Click a category total on each sheet and read the formula bar. A SUMIFS will update when you add expenses. A typed number won't. If either assistant typed values, ask it to use formulas instead.

In practice, both handle a task like this. Copilot is built into Excel and is quick for single-sheet jobs. Claude is strong at multi-sheet reasoning and explaining with citations. The checking effort is the same for both.

acts.t:
Which one for which job
Copilot: built in, quick single-sheet edits, Plan mode, Python analysis
Claude: whole-workbook reasoning, cell citations, model audits, PDFs
Both: answers vary per run; you still check totals and formulas

steps.say: A common mistake is picking a favourite and never checking it. Both assistants make different small mistakes on different days. Your checks, not the brand, make the result safe.

acts.t:
Common mistake
“Claude is better” or “Copilot is better”, so no checks.
Answers vary per run for both.
Always: baseline total, totals match, read formulas, spot-check rows.

steps.say: To recap. Give both the same prompt on separate copies. Compare how they worked and whether they used formulas. And run the same checks on both.

acts.t:
Recap
• Same prompt, separate copies
• Compare: asked first? formulas? explanation?
• Same checks: baseline total, totals, a few rows

steps.say: Your challenge: run one more prompt on both sheets, flag any Meals expense over two thousand rupees, and compare the answers. See the Done sheet for our comparison.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask both: flag any expense over ₹2,000 in Meals and give a reason it might need approval.
Compare the answers and the checking effort.
See sheet S20-10 Done.
